capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user

inputs.source: User's direct chat instruction to the agent
Issue content in the public GitHub repository; any GitHub user can open issues there

instructions.note: The user's request 'Have a look at the open issues in my public repo' does not instruct the agent to treat issue content as untrusted or to refuse embedded instructions, leaving the agent free to act on anything found in issue text.

controls.name: Per-tool-call approval prompt with collapsed arguments
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a model-generated summary behind a collapsed argument view, not the raw destination and payload, so a more persuasive model can write incomplete or misleading summaries (ASI09). High per-session call volume also produces approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Least-privilege credential separation between private-read and public-write operations
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped only to the public repository, with no access to private repositories, would make the private-repo read step unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Pin github-mcp-server image to a digest or fixed version
controls.decay_rationale: A pinned digest stops tool definitions and schemas from changing without an explicit, reviewable configuration update.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): a public issue can direct the agent to read private repo contents and publish them via a public pull request

attack_path.note: Anyone on GitHub can open an issue in the public repo; the agent reads this content while 'looking at open issues'.
Issue text can instruct the agent to call get_file_contents against the user's private repositories, which the PAT (repo scope, all repos) permits.
The agent creates a pull request on the public repo containing private repo contents, making them world-readable.

forecast.watch_signal: Approval review mode stays model_summary while the underlying model is upgraded; the client raises per-session approval volume or auto-approves repeated tool patterns (approval fatigue); or any autonomy change removes or narrows the per-call gate.

evidence.observation: The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so the same credential used for create_pull_request also has read access to private repos.
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, making issue content an untrusted (U) input that reaches the agent's context.
The client asks for approval per tool call but arguments are collapsed by default, which is a model_summary approval gate rather than raw_action review.

recommendations.action: Scope the GitHub credential so that the identity used for create_pull_request (or any public-repo write) has no read access to private repositories; use separate least-privilege tokens for private-read and public-write operations.

Change the approval prompt to raw_action review: show full arguments, including any file contents or diff being posted, by default rather than behind a collapsed link, especially for cross-repository actions.
Log and alert when a single session reads from a private repository and then writes to a public repository.

Treat issue, comment, and PR description content from the public repo as untrusted data; require a separate explicit user confirmation naming the specific private repo and file before any private-repo read triggered by issue content.

findings.title: Unpinned github-mcp-server image allows tool definitions to change without review (ASI04 rug pull)

attack_path.note: docker run pulls ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server with no tag or digest pinned, so the image can change between runs without the user approving a new version.
A changed tool definition could silently alter what get_file_contents does or add hidden parameters.
A changed tool definition could alter create_pull_request behavior, for example the effective target repo or visibility.

forecast.watch_signal: The docker image tag or digest configuration changes, or the tool list/schema returned by the MCP server differs between sessions without a corresponding config diff.

evidence.observation: docker run uses image 'ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server' with no tag or digest specified, which defaults to the latest tag, so tool definitions are not pinned.

recommendations.action: Pin the github-mcp-server image to a specific digest and review the diff before upgrading.

rating.rationale: The dominant path is the lethal trifecta (TC1): any GitHub user can open an issue in the public repo (untrusted input) that instructs the agent to read the user's private repositories (S3, confidential data, via a personal access token scoped across all owned repos) and publish the contents in a pull request on the public repo (S3 egress). Inherent risk is critical. The only control on this path is a per-call human approval prompt that shows a collapsed, model-summarized view of each action rather than raw arguments; this is scored as a partially_dependent structural control, which holds residual at the floor of moderate rather than lower, since no structural control severs the path (the token is not separately scoped for public-write versus private-read). A model upgrade, an increase in autonomy that removes or narrows the per-call gate, or ordinary approval fatigue from high call volume would defeat this gate, returning the risk to critical, which sets the forecast. A secondary, lower-confidence finding notes the MCP server's docker image is unpinned, an ASI04 supply-chain gap that would let a tool-definition change bypass the same approval gate's model-generated summaries.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided MCP config and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the agent or the MCP server.
No system prompt or agent instructions were provided beyond the user's single request; instruction-level findings are limited to what that one request implies.

The actual tool descriptions and schemas served by the github-mcp-server container were not provided, so the tool-poisoning risk in finding f2 is inferred from the lack of image pinning rather than from observed tool definitions.

No confirmation was available of whether the per-tool-call approval prompt fires identically for read-only calls like get_file_contents and for write calls like create_pull_request; the assessment treats both capabilities as gated per the stated runtime notes.
